column2: That encounter, tumultuous, of dreadful form, fierce, took place in the battle between Karna and the Pandava, O lord of men.
Seeing those two great chariot-warriors met, O great king, the thought came to me, "How surely will this turn out today?"
Then in a moment, O king of kings, without much difficulty, as if laughing, Karna made Bhima of terrible deeds chariotless.
Chariotless, the best of the Bharatas, mighty-armed, laughing, wind-like, mace in hand, leapt down from his excellent chariot.
Bhima, scorcher of foes, in a sudden rage, destroyed seven hundred elephants, strikers with plough-pole tusks, O king.
Knowing vital spots, he roared and smashed them hard on the tusk-rings, eyes, temples and vital points.
Then, sent against him again, they fled in fear, and with their chief drivers they surrounded him like clouds the sun.
Standing on the ground he slew with his mace those seven hundred elephants with their riders, weapons and banners, as the wind scatters rain-clouds.
Then the son of Kunti in the battle again crushed fifty-two very strong elephants of Subala's son.
Likewise the Pandava slew over a hundred chariots and hundreds of other foot-soldiers in the battle, scorching your army.
Scorched by the sun and by the great-souled Bhima, your army shrank like hide in fire.
Terrified by fear of Bhima, those of yours, O best of the Bharatas, abandoned Bhima in the battle and fled in all ten directions.
Five hundred other chariots, thundering and armoured with hides, quickly rushed at Bhima on every side with masses of arrows.
Bhima crushed them all, with their charioteers, chariots, pennants, banners and weapons, with his mace, as Vishnu the asuras.
Then three thousand horsemen sent by Shakuni, esteemed as brave, with darts, spears and lances in hand, went against Bhima.
Meeting those Yavana horsemen, the best slayer of foes, moving in various paths, destroyed them, crushing them.
There was a great noise of them struck on all sides, like reeds being cut by swords, O Bharata.
Thus having killed three thousand fine horses of Subala's son, he mounted another chariot and, enraged, went at Radheya.
Karna too in battle, O king, covered the tamer of foes, the son of Dharma, with arrows and felled his charioteer.
Then seeing the chariot fleeing in the battle, the great chariot-warrior pursued it, scattering straight heron-feathered arrows.
As he ran at the king, covering heaven and earth with arrows, the wind's son, enraged, covered him with a net of arrows.
Turning back swiftly, Radheya, tormentor of foes, covered Bhima on every side with sharp arrows.
Satyaki, of immeasurable spirit, tormented Karna, who was busied with Bhimasena's chariot, in order to take his rear; Karna, though greatly tormented by arrows, turned on him.
Meeting each other, those two bulls among all archers, loosing wondrous arrows, shone, high-minded.
From them a net of arrows, dreadful to behold, red-backed like a heron, spread terribly in the sky, O king of kings.
We could not tell the sun's light, the sky or the quarters and intermediate quarters, because of the thousands of arrows loosed by them.
At midday, O king, the great radiance of the blazing sun was entirely obscured by those masses of arrows of Karna and Madhava (Satyaki).
Seeing Subala's son, Kritavarman, Drona's son, Adhiratha's son and Kripa engaged with the Pandavas, the Kurus turned back again.
The sound of them rushing was loud, O lord of men, like the dreadful roar of oceans stirred by a storm.
Seeing each other greatly agitated in the great battle, those two armies, filled with great joy, seized one another.
Then, when the sun reached the middle of the sky, a battle began such as never before seen nor heard.
One flood of troops, meeting another suddenly in battle, rushed with speed like a flood of water to the sea.
There arose a great sound of the floods of troops on each other, like the great roar of floods of oceans.
Those two swift armies, meeting each other, became one, like two rivers at a confluence.
Then began a dreadful battle, O lord of men, of the Kurus and Pandavas seeking great fame.
The voices of the roaring Kurus were heard there without a break, naming many names, O Bharata.
Whatever mark a man had in battle from his father or mother, or from deed or character, he proclaimed it in the fight.
Seeing those heroes in the battle threatening one another, the thought came to me, O king, that they had no life left.
Seeing the bodies of those enraged ones of immeasurable splendour, a great fear arose in me: "How will this turn out?"
Then the Pandavas, O king, and the Kaurava great chariot-warriors hewed at each other with sharp arrows, striking one another.
Masses of chariots, masses of horses, masses of men and masses of elephants, O great king, clashed with one another on every side.
We saw the falling in that most dreadful battle of maces, iron clubs, kanapas, lances, bhindipalas and bhushundis on every side,
and showers of arrows fell on every side like locusts.
Elephants, reaching elephants, struck each other down; horses horses in the battle, chariot-warriors chariot-warriors; foot-soldiers with bands of foot-soldiers, horses with bands of horses.
Foot-soldiers crushed chariots and elephants, chariots horses and elephants, and elephants in the battle swiftly crushed the rest, O king.
With the fall of heroes there and their crying out to one another, the dreadful battlefield became like a slaughter of animals.
The earth, covered with blood, shone, O Bharata, like the earth in the rains strewn with Indra's cochineal insects.
As a young woman might wear two white garments dyed with a great red dye, so the earth became, as if painted with flesh and blood and as if made of gold.
Of severed heads, of arms together with thighs, of hurled earrings and ornaments, O Bharata,
of necklaces, belts, the bodies of archers, armour with banners, heaps fell on the ground there.
Elephants, meeting elephants, tore them with the tips of their tusks, and struck by tusks they shone like wounded elephants.
With their limbs drenched in blood like mountains streaming red ochre, they shone, mountains adorned with minerals.
Javelins hurled by elephants at enemies who stood facing them, the elephants wandered about with their trunks and others broke.
With their armour split by iron arrows, the best elephants shone, O great king, like cloud-covered mountains at the onset of winter.
The best elephants, covered with golden-feathered arrows, shone like mountains with blazing tops of meteors, O revered one.
Some elephants, struck by elephants, fell like mountains to the ground in that battle, like winged mountains.
Other elephants, tormented by arrows and wounds, ran off, and fell to the ground in the great battle, with their temples and tusk-rings.
Others sank down like lions, roaring terrible roars, and many, O king, grew faint and others cried out.
Horses killed by Baka warriors, with golden ornaments and coverings, sank down, grew faint and wandered in all ten directions.
Others, being dragged and writhing on the ground, struck by arrows and javelins, made various gestures.
Men lay slain on the ground, crying out there, O revered one; others, seeing kinsmen, fathers or grandfathers,
and others running, O Bharata, proclaimed their famous clan names to one another.
Their severed arms, adorned with gold, O great king, writhed, twisted, fell and leapt up.
They fell on the ground and twitched by thousands, and some made rapid movements in the battle like quivering snakes.
Those arms, like serpents' coils, anointed with sandal, O lord of men, drenched in blood, shone greatly like golden banners.
While the dreadful confusion went on in every direction, unrecognised they fought, striking one another.
Covered with earth-dust and crowded with falling weapons, neither their own nor the enemy, O king, were recognised in the darkness.
Thus that dreadful, terrible battle went on, and great rivers of blood flowed there again and again.
Covered with heads and stones, with hair for moss and grass, filled with heaps of bones, with bows and the best of arrows,
with mud of flesh and floods of blood, most dreadful, they made rivers flow that increased the realm of Yama.
Those dreadful rivers, carrying men to Yama's abode, plunging and drowning them, struck fear into the kshatriyas.
With flesh-eaters roaring here and there, O tiger among men, the dreadful battlefield became like the city of the king of the dead.
Innumerable headless trunks rose on every side, and hosts of spirits danced, satisfied with flesh and blood.
Having drunk blood and fat, O Bharata, fed on marrow, fat and flesh, crows, vultures and herons were seen running.
Those heroes in battle, O king, giving up fear, which is hard to give up, did their deeds fearlessly, true to a warrior's vow.
In the field strewn with arrows and darts and thronged by flesh-eaters, brave heroes ranged in bands, proclaiming their own manliness.
They announced to one another their names and clans, and the names of their fathers and clans, in the battle, O Bharata.
Many warriors there, proclaiming, crushed one another with darts, javelins and pattishas, O lord of men.
While that dreadful, most terrible battle went on, the Kaurava army sank, like a broken ship in the sea.
Where the Pandava slaughtered the Samshaptakas, and likewise the Kosalas and the Narayana force, O king—
the Samshaptakas, eager for victory and in great rage, rained a shower of arrows on Partha's head from every side in the battle.
The lord swiftly bore that shower, O king, and entered the battle, slaying, best of chariot-warriors.
Having checked the chariot-force with stone-whetted heron-feathered arrows, Partha reached the great chariot-warrior Susharma in the battle.
The best of chariot-warriors rained showers of arrows on him, and the Samshaptakas too stood in the battle against Partha.
Then Susharma, piercing Partha with nine swift arrows and Janardana with three, struck him on the right arm, and with another broad-headed arrow pierced the standard, O revered one.
That excellent monkey, the great one made by Vishvakarma, uttered a great cry, frightening, and roared.
Hearing the monkey's roar, your army, terrified, took on great fear and became motionless.
Then that army shone, standing motionless, O king, like the Chaitraratha forest strewn with flowers of many kinds.
Regaining consciousness, the warriors, best of the Kurus, showered Arjuna with arrows as clouds on a mountain, and all surrounded the Pandava's great chariot.
They quickly held the horses, wheels and poles of the chariot by force, O Bharata, and roared lion-roars.
Others seized Keshava's mighty arms, and others, O great king, joyfully seized Partha on his chariot.
Then Keshava, shaking his arms at the head of the battle, threw them all down like a vicious elephant its fellow elephants.
Then Partha, enraged in battle and surrounded by those great chariot-warriors, seeing his chariot held and Keshava attacked, felled many chariot-borne and foot-soldiers.
He dislodged the warriors who stood close with arrows in the battle by close fighters, and said this to Keshava:

See, Krishna, mighty-armed, the Samshaptaka hosts doing dreadful deeds and being slain by me in thousands.
mahabharata:8:37.18	This dreadful binding of the chariot—there is no one on earth, O bull of the Yadus, who could bear it other than I.
Having said this, Bibhatsu blew Devadatta, and Krishna too blew Panchajanya, as if filling heaven and earth.
Hearing that conch-sound, the Samshaptaka host trembled, O great king, and was greatly terrified.
Then the Pandava, slayer of heroes, O great king, repeatedly invoking the Naga weapon, made the foot-binding.
Those at whom Partha aimed the foot-binding in the battle were bound by the foot-binding of the great-souled Pandava and became motionless, O king, as if made of stone.
The son of Pandu then slew the motionless warriors, as the moon in battle slew the daityas at the slaying of Taraka long ago.
Being slain in the battle, they released that excellent chariot and began to cast away all their weapons.
Then, O king of kings, seeing his army seized, Susharma, the great chariot-warrior, swiftly brought forth the Suparna weapon.
Then Suparnas (Garudas) fell upon them, devouring serpents, and the serpents fled on seeing those sky-ranging birds, O king.
That army, freed from the foot-binding, O lord of men, shone like the sun freed from a mass of clouds, scorching creatures.
Freed, those warriors poured masses of arrows and masses of weapons on Phalguna's chariot, O revered one.
Cutting that rain of great weapons with showers of arrows, the son of Vasava, slayer of heroes, stood facing the warriors.
Then Susharma, O king, with a bent-jointed arrow, pierced Arjuna in the heart and with three more arrows; deeply pierced, he sat down on his chariot-seat, pained.
Regaining consciousness, the white-horsed one with Krishna as charioteer, of immeasurable spirit, swiftly brought forth Indra's weapon; then thousands of arrows were produced, O revered one.
They were seen in all directions, killing elephants, horses and chariots in battle, O king, with weapons by the hundred thousand.
As the army was being slain, great fear entered the Samshaptaka hosts and the Gopalas, O Bharata; there was no man there who fought Arjuna.
In the sight of heroes there, the great army was slain; they saw it being slain and stood motionless in their valour.
Having slain ten thousand warriors there in battle, the son of Pandu shone in battle, O king, like a smokeless blazing fire.
Fourteen thousand remained, O Bharata, and ten thousand chariots and three thousand elephants.
Then the Samshaptakas surrounded Dhananjaya again, resolved to die or to win.
A great battle took place there, O lord of men, between your men and the strong hero, the Pandava Kiritin.
Seeing the army sinking, tormented by fear of the son of Pandu, wishing to lift it swiftly like a broken ship in the sea,
then the battle became exceedingly great for a moment, O Bharata, striking fear into the timid and increasing the joy of the brave.
The Srinjayas cut down in the battle the showers of arrows loosed by Kripa, like flights of locusts.
Then Shikhandin, enraged, swiftly went to Gautama (Kripa), raining showers of arrows on the Brahmana on every side.
Kripa, skilled in great weapons, having warded off that shower of arrows, enraged, pierced Shikhandin in the battle with ten arrows.
Then the angered Shikhandin pierced Kripa hard in the battle with seven straight heron-feathered arrows.
Then Kripa, deeply pierced by sharp arrows, that great chariot-warrior, best of the twice-born, made the Parshata's chariot horseless and charioteerless.
Leaping from the chariot whose horses were slain, the great chariot-warrior took shield and sword and quickly went to the Brahmana.
As he suddenly came, he covered him with straight-jointed arrows in the battle; it was wondrous.
We saw there a marvel like stones floating: that Shikhandin stood motionless in the battle, O king.
Seeing Shikhandin covered by Kripa, the great chariot-warrior Dhrishtadyumna, best of kings, swiftly advanced against Kripa.
As Dhrishtadyumna went towards Sharadvata's chariot, the great chariot-warrior Kritavarman quickly confronted him.
As Yudhishthira advanced towards Sharadvata's chariot with his sons and troops, Drona's son held him back.
Your son confronted the two great chariot-warriors Nakula and Sahadeva in haste, holding them back with showers of arrows.
Karna Vaikartana in the battle held back Bhimasena, the Karushas, Kekayas and Srinjayas, O Bharata.
Then Kripa Sharadvata, in haste, as if wishing to burn him, sent arrows at Shikhandin in the battle, O revered one.
He cut those arrows, sent by him, adorned with gold, from every side with his sword, brandishing and whirling it again and again.
Then Gautama quickly shattered the Parshata's shield marked with a hundred moons with arrows, and the people cried out.
Shieldless, O great king, with sword in hand, he ran forward, falling under Kripa's power like a sick man into the mouth of death.
Seeing the mighty one tormented, swallowed up by Sharadvata's arrows, Suketu, son of Chitraketu, quickly went there, O king.
Scattering many sharp arrows at the Brahmana in the battle, the one of immeasurable spirit attacked Gautama's chariot.
Seeing that Brahmana, practised in vows, irresistible in battle, Shikhandin, best of kings, quickly retreated.
Then Suketu, O king, piercing Gautama with nine arrows, again pierced him with seventy and again with three.
Then, O revered one, he cut his bow with its arrow once more and struck his charioteer hard in a vital part with an arrow.
Gautama, enraged, taking a new firm bow, struck Suketu in all his vital parts with thirty arrows.
With all his limbs bewildered, he swayed on the best of chariots, like a tree shaken hard in an earthquake.
As he swayed, Kripa struck off with a razor-arrow from his body his head with blazing earrings, turban and helmet.
That head fell to the ground like meat carried off by a hawk; afterwards his body, fallen, reached the earth.
When he was slain, O great king, his followers, terrified, abandoned Gautama in the battle and fled in all ten directions.
The mighty Kritavarman, having held back Dhrishtadyumna in the battle, said boldly to the Parshata, "Stand, stand!"
A tumultuous battle took place between the Vrishni and the Parshata in the fight, like the battle of two hawks or vultures over meat, O king.
Dhrishtadyumna, enraged, in battle struck Hardikya in the chest with nine arrows, tormenting the son of Hridika.
Kritavarman, firmly struck in battle by the Parshata, covered the Parshata with his chariot and horses with arrows.
Covered with his chariot, O king, Dhrishtadyumna was not seen, like the sun hidden by clouds at the coming of the rains.
Shaking off that mass of arrows with gold-adorned arrows, Dhrishtadyumna shone in the battle, O king, though wounded.
Then the Parshata, enraged, reaching Kritavarman, the army's leader, loosed a most dreadful shower of weapons.
That uninterrupted shower of weapons, suddenly falling, Hardikya destroyed in the battle with many thousands of arrows.
Seeing that hard-to-cross shower of weapons torn apart in the battle, the Parshata approached Kritavarman and held him back.
He swiftly sent his charioteer to Yama's abode with a sharp-edged broad-headed arrow, and he fell dead from the chariot.
Dhrishtadyumna, the strong one, having conquered the great chariot-warrior foe, quickly held back the Kauravas in the battle with arrows.
Then your warriors ran at Dhrishtadyumna, raising lion-roars, and the battle began.
Scattering fierce masses of golden-feathered arrows whetted on stone, showing paths of many kinds for practice, quick-handed,
he filled the sky with arrows consecrated with divine weapon-mantras, and the knower of weapons surrounded Yudhishthira in the battle.
Covered by Drona's son's arrows, nothing could be distinguished; the whole battlefield head became as if made of arrows.
That net of arrows in the sky, adorned with a net of gold, shone, O best of the Bharatas, like a canopy spread out.
Covered by that shining net of arrows, O king, a shade as of clouds arose, the sky blocked by arrows.
There, in that sky made of arrows, we saw the wonder that nothing fell to the ground, seeing Drona's son's prowess.
Seeing the dexterity of Drona's son, the great chariot-warriors there were astonished, O great king, and all the kings could not look at him, as at the blazing sun.
Satyaki, striving, and the Pandava king of dharma and the other armies did not display valour.
While the army was being slain, the sons of Draupadi, great chariot-warriors, Satyaki, the king of dharma and the Panchalas together, giving up the terrible fear of death, rushed at Drona's son.
Satyaki, piercing Drona's son with twenty-five stone-faced arrows, pierced him again with seven gold-adorned iron arrows.
Yudhishthira with seventy-three, Pratívindhya with seven, Shrutakarman with three arrows, Shrutakirti with seven,
Sutasoma with nine, Shatanika with seven, and many other brave ones pierced him on every side.
Greatly enraged, then, O king, sighing like a venomous serpent, he pierced Satyaki with twenty-five stone-whetted arrows.
And he wept, "Alas, king!" in grief, O tiger among men. "Ah, we are greatly distressed at the death of the great soul."
[Sanjaya said:] Going on, O king, your men stopped not far away and saw a dreadful forest full of trees and creepers of many kinds.
I do not remember any evil I did earlier, Sanjaya, of which I, deluded, now enjoy the fruit here.
Draupadi, whose sons are slain, wretched, her kinsmen slain, though devoted to what is dear and good to us, seems to afflict me further.
Those light in dharma float in the world as in water; those heavy with sin sink, like a dropped weapon in water.
If you do not wish the son of Kunti, Yudhishthira, as king, then take the kingdom yourself, O king, as a puppet.
Cooks, soup-makers and music-makers attended King Dhritarashtra as before.
This Samba will bear a dreadful iron pestle for the destruction of the Vrishnis and Andhakas, descendants of Vasudeva.
Then that Kuru king, Yudhishthira, son of Dharma, laying aside the ornaments from his body, took up garments of bark.
Meet King Duryodhana as is fitting; this is heaven; here enmities do not exist, O lord of men.
